strengths: Maximizing incremental benefit is a relevant objective for influence maximization. Allowing heterogeneous and negative treatment effects captures practical cases where increased reach does not necessarily improve outcomes.
The modular combination of treatment-effect estimation and hypergraph seed selection is understandable and potentially useful.

The reported experiments show substantial gains over unweighted CELF and random selection on the chosen benchmark, with repeated runs and additional noise, propagation-probability, and runtime analyses.
weaknesses: The main approximation guarantee is not established by the supplied proof. Appendix B, Equation (6), adds contributions separately across seeds and therefore double-counts shared reachable nodes. Equation (14) also incorrectly bounds the accumulated error: at K=15, the displayed penalty sum has coefficient approximately 5.329, whereas its proposed replacement exp(1/K−1) is approximately 0.393. These are substantive errors affecting Theorem 5.5.

The implemented CELF variant lacks justification for signed rewards. When submodularity fails, previously computed marginal gains need not upper-bound current gains, so lazy selection can differ from full greedy selection. Nevertheless, the paper transfers greedy guarantees to CELF. The robustness proof also uses multiplicative-error inequalities that are not valid as written for negative objective values, while division by the objective is undefined at zero.

The causal formulation is insufficiently coherent. Assumption 3.2 excludes outcome interference, while the estimator explicitly models interference through neighboring treatments. The manuscript does not reconcile these choices or establish why effects estimated under observed neighboring treatments remain appropriate after seed interventions change the treatment configuration. An overlap assumption is also missing from the identification argument.

The evaluation is limited to simulated effects on one Goodreads subgraph, approximately 4,400 nodes and 120 hyperedges. Comparisons only with unweighted CELF and random selection do not establish an advantage over methods optimizing the same weighted objective. There are no oracle-effect comparisons, effect-estimation accuracy results, or targeted evaluations of negative-effect regimes. It is unclear whether reported rewards use true simulated effects or fitted estimates. Reward-variance plots alone do not establish robustness of achieved causal benefit.

Important modeling and reproducibility details remain unresolved. Section 3.1 specifies independent-cascade activation, Section 4.1 describes repeated hyperedge selection, and Appendix A uses an SI/contact process; their equivalence is not established. Algorithm 4 uses the same parameter for simulation repetitions and diffusion depth, confounding estimation accuracy with propagation duration. Subgraph selection, effect-generation details, and estimator training settings are insufficiently specified.

The demonstrated originality is limited beyond combining existing components: the estimator follows Ma et al. [25], and seed selection uses weighted greedy/CELF machinery. The blanket claim that existing influence-maximization methods optimize only node counts conflicts with the cited weighted influence-maximization work [36]. Without a valid new guarantee or stronger comparative evidence, the potentially useful integration does not support acceptance.
